title: When the Gestapo Raided the Villa Seurat
author: Jeffrey St. Clair
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/P1110202_Paris_XIV_villa_Seurat_rwk-680x513.jpg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/08/19/when-
the-gestapo-raided-the-villa-seurat/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/P1110202_Paris_XIV_villa_Seurat_rwk-680x513.jpg)

Villa Seurat, XIV Arrondissement. Wikimedia. [CC BY
3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0/).

In 1930, Henry Miller arrived in Paris with only a razor, toothbrush, pen,
notebook and walking stick to his name. He set up shop on the Villa Seurat, a
short cul-de-sac street in the 14th arrondissement, near the writers Anais Nin
and his sometimes housemate, Lawrence Durrell, as well as the painter Chaim
Soutine.

It was here that Miller began to write _Tropic of Cancer._ It was also here
that Miller became so obsessed with astrology that he painted his astrological
chart on the wall of his room. He would spend many evenings on the roof of the
house, scanning the heavens with his telescope. One night he became so
entranced by his planetary observations that he stepped onto the building’s
skylight, breaking through the glass and falling down more than 20 feet to a
hard landing on the floor. Somehow he emerged with only a few cuts and bruises
from a fall that could have killed him.

Miller consulted his astrologer, a certain Morcard, on the meaning of the
episode. Morcard asked Miller what planet or constellation he was looking at
when he fell.

“Jupiter,” Miller replied.

“Ah,” said Morcad, nodding his head. “That means Jupiter is your protector!”

To make money, the perpetually skinflint Miller started writing an astrology
column and dispatches on Paris’s fashion scene for a publication called _La
Revue Officielle de la Villa Seurat,_ where Nin wrote the society and gossip
columns and Durrell served as the zine’s sports reporter. What sort of sports,
I’ll leave to your imagination.

Miller escaped the Nazi occupation, but his letters, notes, drafts of his
novels and likely some of the porn he was being paid by the word to write
didn’t. The Nazis confiscated Miller’s papers when they raided the Villa
Seurat in search of Soutine, but the Jewish painter had already fled occupied
Paris.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/soutineself-680x688.png)

Self-Portrait (Detail), Chaïm Soutine. 1918. The Henry and Rose Pearlman
Foundation, on long-term loan to the Princeton University Art Museum. Public
Domain.

Soutine had barely escaped the Gestapo and spent the last two years of his
abbreviated life on the run, sleeping in forests, barns, abandoned buildings,
in rural motels under fake documents, always in fear of being discovered or,
worse, secretly denounced. Still, he continued to sketch and paint. His
landscapes became darker and more distorted, almost warped, with each passing
month. The faces of his portraits twisted with anguish, the eyes reflecting
the descending darkness.

In the summer of 1943, Soutine, stressed out from being hunted, the paranoid
outbursts of his lover Marie-Berthe Aurenche, and impoverishment, developed an
ulcer. For weeks he could eat only porridge and he often could keep that
meager meal down. Eventually, the ulcer perforated his stomach lining and the
pain grew so intense that he was forced to leave his sanctuary in the Chinon
commune of the Loire Valley for a desperate flight to Paris, seeking emergency
surgery. But he arrived too late. Chaim Soutine bled to death on the operating
table. He was 50 years old.
